propositions.text: SOCAN initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board to set royalty rates for 2014–2026 for online audiovisual and user-generated content services.
propositions.quote: The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board seeking an order of the Board establishing the royalty rates (i.e., setting tariffs) SOCAN will collect for 2014–2026 from users of musical works in online audiovisual services and user-generated content services.

propositions.text: The Copyright Board has authority to set such rates under the Copyright Act.
propositions.quote: The Copyright Board has the authority to set such rates under the Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42.

paragraphs.summary: The Copyright Board proceeding was initiated by SOCAN to set royalty rates for 2014–2026 under the Copyright Act, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The Board divided the proceeding into two phases and identified four preliminary issues for Phase I.
propositions.quote: During case management, the Board decided to divide the proceeding into two phases and identified “four preliminary issues” to be considered in Phase I

propositions.text: The four preliminary issues concern applicability of CBC v SODRAC, statutory exceptions, interpretation of paragraph 66.501(a), and rights triggered by offline viewing copies.
propositions.quote: 1. Does the Supreme Court’s decision in CBC v SODRAC, 2015 SCC 57, apply to tariff proceedings before the Board? ... 4. When offline viewing copies are offered, created, and used, which rights are triggered?

paragraphs.summary: The Board divided the proceeding into two phases and identified four preliminary issues for Phase I, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The Board included two safeguards in Phase I Notice; the second allows reconsideration if Phase II evidence casts doubt on Phase I conclusions.
propositions.quote: The second of those safeguards, relevant to this matter, was that “if evidence in Phase II significantly throws into doubt a conclusion from Phase I, parties can ask the Board to reconsider that conclusion”

paragraphs.summary: The Board included a safeguard allowing reconsideration of Phase I conclusions if Phase II evidence casts doubt, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: On Nov 21, 2025, the Board issued a Phase I Ruling with preliminary conclusions, not final determinations on tariffs.
propositions.quote: On November 21, 2025, the Board issued a ruling setting out its “conclusions on these preliminary issues” stating the ruling “does not constitute [the Board’s] final determinations on the Proposed Tariffs under consideration”

propositions.text: The Board reminded parties of the safeguard allowing reconsideration if Phase II evidence casts doubt on Phase I conclusions.
propositions.quote: The Board also reminded the parties of its safeguard that “if evidence in Phase II significantly throws into doubt a conclusion from Phase I, parties can ask the Board to reconsider that conclusion”

paragraphs.summary: The Board issued a Phase I Ruling with preliminary conclusions and reminded parties of the reconsideration safeguard, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.
propositions.quote: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling, says the applicant.

propositions.text: Respondents argue the Phase I Ruling is interlocutory and not judicially reviewable.
propositions.quote: They contend that the Phase I Ruling is an interlocutory one in a larger and ongoing administrative process and is therefore not a “decision” amenable to judicial review

propositions.text: Respondents argue SOCAN has not exhausted adequate alternative recourse.
propositions.quote: that even if it were a decision that could be judicially reviewed in principle, SOCAN has not exhausted adequate and effective alternative recourse

propositions.text: Respondents argue no exceptional circumstances justify early judicial intervention.
propositions.quote: and that no exceptional circumstances exist to justify early judicial intervention

propositions.text: Respondents seek lump sum or heightened costs, arguing SOCAN’s application should not have been brought.
propositions.quote: These respondents seek lump sum costs of $20,000, or costs on a heightened basis, on the ground SOCAN’s application should never have been brought.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue the Phase I Ruling is interlocutory, SOCAN has not exhausted recourse, no exceptional circumstances exist, and seek costs, says the respondent.

propositions.text: SOCAN disagrees but says if respondents succeed, costs should be $5,000, not heightened.
propositions.quote: SOCAN has a different view of the matter. However, it contends that if the respondents’ motion is successful, heightened costs are not justified and that a $5,000 costs award is more appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN disagrees but says if respondents succeed, costs should be $5,000, not heightened, says the applicant.

propositions.text: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the judicial review application.
propositions.quote: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: I agree respondents are entitled to costs but $5,000 is appropriate, not heightened costs.
propositions.quote: While I agree the respondents are entitled to costs, I agree with SOCAN that a costs award of $5,000 is more appropriate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: I would grant the motion to strike, dismiss the application, and award $5,000 costs, says the court.

propositions.text: To succeed on a motion to strike, respondents must show the application is clearly improper with no possibility of success.
propositions.quote: To succeed in this motion, the respondents must demonstrate that SOCAN’s application for judicial review is “so clearly improper as to be bereft of any possibility of success”

propositions.text: This is a high threshold, citing JP Morgan and David Bull Laboratories.
propositions.quote: This is admittedly a high threshold to meet.

paragraphs.summary: To succeed on a motion to strike, respondents must show the application is clearly improper with no chance of success, a high threshold, says the court.

propositions.text: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike except documents in the notice or incorporated by reference.
propositions.quote: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike, and with limited exceptions, we must presume the facts asserted in the notice of application are true; documents referred to in the notice of application or incorporated by reference can be taken into account

propositions.text: Documents include Phase I Notice, Phase I Ruling, and earlier Board ruling CB-CDA 2025-004.
propositions.quote: Here, those documents include the Phase I Notice and the Phase I Ruling, as well as an earlier Board ruling, CB-CDA 2025-004 dated January 16, 2025.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike except documents in the notice or incorporated by reference, including Phase I Notice and Ruling, says the court.

propositions.text: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties must exhaust administrative process before court.
propositions.quote: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties to an administrative process cannot proceed to the court system until that process has run its course

propositions.text: This principle is supported by C.B. Powell and Dugré.
propositions.quote: Canada (Border Services Agency) v. C.B. Powell Limited, 2010 FCA 61 at para. 31 [C.B. Powell]; Dugré v. Canada (Attorney General), 2021 FCA 8 at paras. 34, 37 [Dugré].

paragraphs.summary: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties must exhaust administrative process before court, says prior authorities cited by the court.

propositions.text: This principle applies to all matters before the administrative decision maker.
propositions.quote: This principle applies “to all matters that arise” before the administrative decision maker

propositions.text: Procedural fairness concerns do not meet exceptional circumstances threshold.
propositions.quote: A procedural fairness concern does not meet the “exceptional circumstances” threshold

propositions.text: These rules are supported by Klos and Herbert.
propositions.quote: Klos v. Canada (Attorney General), 2021 FCA 238 at para. 6. A procedural fairness concern does not meet the “exceptional circumstances” threshold: Herbert v. Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FCA 11 at para. 11.

paragraphs.summary: The principle applies to all administrative matters; procedural fairness concerns do not meet exceptional circumstances, says prior authorities cited by the court.

propositions.text: The rule prevents fragmentation, costs, delays, and waste from premature court proceedings.
propositions.quote: The purpose of this rule is to prevent “fragmentation of the administrative process and piecemeal court proceedings”, to eliminate “the large costs and delays associated with premature forays to court”, and to avoid “the waste associated with hearing an interlocutory judicial review when the applicant for judicial review may succeed at the end of the administrative process anyway”

propositions.text: These purposes are supported by C.B. Powell and Dugré.
propositions.quote: C.B. Powell at para. 32, cited in Dugré at para. 34.

paragraphs.summary: The rule prevents fragmentation, costs, delays, and waste from premature court proceedings, says prior authorities cited by the court.

propositions.text: To bypass administrative process, interlocutory decision consequences must be immediate and radical to question rule of law.
propositions.quote: the consequences of an interlocutory decision [must] be so ‘immediate and radical’ that they call into question the rule of law

propositions.text: This is supported by Dugré and Wilson.
propositions.quote: Dugré at para. 35, quoting from Wilson v. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, 2015 FCA 17 at paras. 31–33 [Wilson].

paragraphs.summary: To bypass administrative process, interlocutory decision consequences must be immediate and radical, says prior authorities cited by the court.

propositions.text: SOCAN seeks order quashing Phase I Ruling and declarations on procedural fairness, errors, issue timing, and exceptions.
propositions.quote: SOCAN’s notice of application seeks an order quashing the Phase I Ruling as well as various declarations, including declarations that (i) the Board failed to discharge its duty of procedural fairness by deciding an issue that was outside the scope of Phase I; (ii) the Board erred in fact and law or reached a decision that is unreasonable; (iii) the Board shall not decide certain issues until the completion of Phase II; and (iv) two exceptions in the Copyright Act do not apply in particular circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN seeks to quash Phase I Ruling and declarations on procedural fairness, errors, issue timing, and exceptions, says the applicant.

propositions.text: Respondents persuaded me SOCAN’s judicial review application is premature.
propositions.quote: the respondents have persuaded me that that threshold is met here. I find SOCAN’s application for judicial review premature for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: I find SOCAN’s judicial review application premature, persuaded by respondents, says the court.

propositions.text: Only administrative action affecting rights, legal obligations, or prejudicial effects is judicially reviewable.
propositions.quote: only administrative action that affects rights, imposes legal obligations, or causes prejudicial effects is amenable to judicial review

propositions.text: This rule is supported by Democracy Watch, Tsleil-Waututh Nation, Air Canada, Canadian Council for Refugees, and Air Passenger Rights.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch v. Canada (Attorney General), 2020 FCA 69 at para. 19; Tsleil-Waututh Nation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 153 at paras. 175–176, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 38379 (2 May 2019); Democracy Watch v. Canada (Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner), 2009 FCA 15 at para. 10 [Democracy Watch]; Air Canada v. Toronto Port Authority Et Al, 2011 FCA 347 at para. 29 [Toronto Port Authority]; (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Canadian Council for Refugees, 2021 FCA 72 at para. 94 [Canadian Council for Refugees]; Air Passenger Rights v. Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FCA 128 paras. 18–31.

paragraphs.summary: Only administrative action affecting rights, obligations, or prejudicial effects is judicially reviewable, supported by prior authorities, says the court.

propositions.text: Phase I Ruling does not affect legal rights or impose obligations warranting judicial review now.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded the Phase I Ruling affects legal rights, imposes legal obligations, or causes prejudicial effects to SOCAN that warrant judicial review at this stage of the proceeding.

propositions.text: Phase I Ruling may affect proceeding balance but is like many interlocutory orders.
propositions.quote: While I accept that the Phase I Ruling may affect the way the balance of the proceeding to determine the tariffs is conducted, that may be said of many interlocutory orders.

paragraphs.summary: Phase I Ruling does not affect legal rights warranting review now; it may affect proceeding balance but is like many interlocutory orders, says the court.

propositions.text: SOCAN argues Phase I decision is final in substance, not manipulation of prematurity doctrine.
propositions.quote: SOCAN posits that the Board’s decision is final in substance no matter how the Board describes it. In doing so, SOCAN says it is not suggesting that the Board intended to manipulate the prematurity doctrine.

propositions.text: SOCAN relies on Federal Court cases where decision makers tried to shield from judicial review.
propositions.quote: Yet, it relies on Federal Court decisions where the relevant administrative decision maker was seen as trying to shield itself from judicial review: Whalen v. Fort McMurray No. 468 First Nation, 2019 FC 732 at para. 23, and GCT Canada Limited Partnership v. Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, 2020 FC 1062 at para. 44, appeal dismissed, 2021 FCA 183.

propositions.text: Circumstances here are not comparable to those cases.
propositions.quote: The circumstances at issue here are simply not comparable to those addressed in those cases.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN argues Phase I decision is final in substance and cites cases of shielding from review; I find circumstances here not comparable, says applicant and court.

propositions.text: SOCAN submits this Court recognized first order of Board in bifurcated proceeding as reviewable.
propositions.quote: SOCAN also submits that this Court has previously recognized a first order of the Board in a bifurcated proceeding as a matter amenable to judicial review.

propositions.text: I agree CAIP is distinguishable for three reasons: finality, consent, and later authorities.
propositions.quote: But I agree with the respondents that Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Canadian Assn. of Internet Providers (C.A.), 2002 FCA 166 [CAIP] is distinguishable. First, the decision under review in CAIP—the Board’s first decision in a bifurcated proceeding—disentitled SOCAN from collecting royalties from an entire class of users and thus was final in that respect: CAIP at paras. 2, 4, 23. Second, the parties consented to the Court’s jurisdiction, and prematurity was not addressed: CAIP at paras. 33–34. Finally, CAIP predates Democracy Watch, Toronto Port Authority, and Canadian Council for Refugees.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN submits prior Court recognized first Board order as reviewable; I find CAIP distinguishable for finality, consent, and later authorities, says applicant and court.

propositions.text: SOCAN's reliance on Wilson is misplaced because Wilson involved a bifurcation creating a natural break between merits and remedy phases.
propositions.quote: I also agree with the respondents that SOCAN’s reliance on Wilson is misplaced. In Wilson the administrative decision maker bifurcated the proceeding into a merits and remedy phase—creating a “natural break between two separate phases of the proceedings”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN's reliance on Wilson misplaced because Wilson involved a natural break between merits and remedy phases.

propositions.text: Here, the Board bifurcated the proceeding but has not yet applied legal interpretations from Phase I, so Phase I and II together concern merits.
propositions.quote: In contrast, here the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties but has yet to apply the legal interpretations set out in its Phase I Ruling.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board bifurcated the proceeding but Phase I and II together concern the merits.

propositions.text: Even if Phase I Ruling were reviewable, SOCAN has not exhausted alternative remedies as Phase I is preliminary and allows reconsideration.
propositions.quote: Second, even if the Phase I Ruling were amenable to judicial review in principle, SOCAN has not exhausted the available alternative remedies.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN has not exhausted alternative remedies because Phase I is preliminary and allows reconsideration.

propositions.text: SOCAN alleges the Board's safeguard is inadequate because legal questions cannot be doubted by evidence and Phase I limits evidence in Phase II.
propositions.quote: SOCAN alleges that the Board’s safeguard is inadequate and ineffective for two reasons. First, insofar as the Phase I Ruling addresses questions of law, they cannot be thrown into doubt by evidence. Second, the Board’s conclusions will limit the evidence that may be tendered in Phase II.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN alleges the Board's safeguard is inadequate because legal questions cannot be doubted by evidence and Phase I limits evidence in Phase II.

propositions.text: The Board is master of its procedure with broad discretion and powers under the Copyright Act and Rules of Practice.
propositions.quote: the Board is the master of its own procedure: Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency (Access Copyright) v. Canada, 2018 FCA 58 at para. 171. More specifically, the Board has broad discretion and powers concerning its processes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board has broad discretion and powers over its procedures under the Copyright Act and Rules.

propositions.text: The Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties as part of its case management.
propositions.quote: the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties as part of its case management, as it was empowered to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties as part of case management.

propositions.text: SOCAN can raise issues before the Board in case management or Phase II and has not exhausted this alternative remedy.
propositions.quote: I see nothing that precludes SOCAN from raising the matters it seeks to raise in its application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling before the Board

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN can raise issues before the Board and has not exhausted this alternative remedy.

propositions.text: There are no exceptional circumstances justifying early court recourse as Phase I Ruling consequences are not immediate or radical.
propositions.quote: there are no exceptional circumstances that would justify early recourse to the courts in respect of the Phase I Ruling. The consequences of the Phase I Ruling, as an interlocutory one, cannot be described in the terms outlined in Dugré and Wilson

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no exceptional circumstances justify early court recourse as Phase I Ruling consequences are not immediate or radical.

propositions.text: Even constitutional or jurisdictional questions cannot attract interlocutory relief; circumstances here are not exceptional.
propositions.quote: this Court has held that “even constitutional questions or questions qualified as ‘jurisdictional’ questions cannot attract interlocutory relief”

paragraphs.summary: The court states constitutional or jurisdictional questions cannot attract interlocutory relief; circumstances here are not exceptional.

propositions.text: SOCAN may succeed at Phase II or later raise the same challenges by judicial review.
propositions.quote: at the end of Phase II, SOCAN may succeed in obtaining the tariffs it seeks

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN may succeed at Phase II or later raise the same challenges by judicial review.

propositions.text: If SOCAN can raise issues before the Board but does not, court may decline to consider them on judicial review.
propositions.quote: If it does not, but could have, it risks this Court exercising its discretion to not consider the issue on a subsequent application for judicial review

paragraphs.summary: The court states if SOCAN can raise issues before the Board but does not, court may decline to consider them on judicial review.

propositions.text: The motion to strike is granted and the judicial review application dismissed without prejudice to SOCAN's right to seek review after Phase II.
propositions.quote: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the application for judicial review. And, while it should be clear from these reasons, I reiterate that if SOCAN decides, upon completion of the administrative process, to seek judicial review of the Phase II decision, this dismissal is without prejudice

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the motion to strike and dismisses the judicial review application without prejudice to SOCAN's right after Phase II.

propositions.text: Costs are awarded to the three respondents in the lump sum amount of $5,000.
propositions.quote: I would award costs to the three respondents in the lump sum all-inclusive amount of $5,000.

paragraphs.summary: The court awards costs to the three respondents in the lump sum amount of $5,000.
